post_theatre_basement_poster_tube.title: Film poster
sents: lead
A film poster is a poster used to promote and advertise a film primarily to persuade paying customers into a theater to see it.
lead
Studios often print several posters that vary in size and content for various domestic and international markets.
lead
They normally contain an image with text.
lead
Today's posters often feature printed likenesses of the main actors.
lead
Prior to the 1980s, illustrations instead of photos were far more common.
lead
The text on film posters usually contains the film title in large lettering and often the names of the main actors.
lead
It may also include a tagline, the name of the director, names of characters, the release date, and other pertinent details to inform prospective viewers about the film.
lead
Film posters are often displayed inside and on the outside of movie theaters, and elsewhere on the street or in shops.
History

The first poster for a specific film, rather than a "magic lantern show", was based on an illustration by Marcellin Auzolle to promote the showing of the Lumiere Brothers film L'Arroseur arrosé at the Grand Café in Paris on December 26, 1895.
History

Originally, film posters were produced for the exclusive use by the theaters exhibiting the film the poster was created for, and were required to be returned to the distributor after the film left the theater.
History

In the United States, film posters were usually returned to a nationwide operation called the National Screen Service (NSS) which printed and distributed most of the film posters for the studios between 1940 and 1984.
History

During this time, a film could stay in circulation for several years, and so many old film posters were badly worn before being retired into storage at an NSS warehouse (most often, they were thrown away when they were no longer needed or had become too worn to be used again).
Collecting

After the National Screen Service ceased most of its printing and distribution operations in 1985, some of the posters which they had stored in warehouses around the United States ended up in the hands of private collectors and dealers.
Collecting

The first auction by a major auction house solely of film posters occurred on December 11, 1990, when proceeds of a sale of 271 vintage posters run by Bruce Hershenson at Christie's totaled US$935,000.
Collecting
The record price for a single poster was set on November 15, 2005, when $690,000 was paid for a poster of Fritz Lang 's 1927 film Metropolis from the Reel Poster Gallery in London.
Collecting

Other early horror and science fiction posters are known to bring extremely high prices as well, with an example from The Mummy realizing $452,000 in a 1997 Sotheby's auction, and posters from both Bride of Frankenstein and The Black Cat selling for $334,600 in Heritage Auctions, in 2007 and 2009, respectively.
Collecting
Occasionally, rare film posters have been found being used as insulation in attics and walls.
Collecting

In 2011, 33 film posters, including a Dracula Style F one-sheet (shown right), from 1930 to 1931 were discovered in an attic in Berwick, Pennsylvania and auctioned for $502,000 in March 2012 by Heritage Auctions.
Collecting
Ghanaian hand-painted movie posters from the tradition's Golden Age in the 1980s and 1990s have sold for tens of thousands of dollars and been exhibited in galleries and museums across the world.
Collecting
Original film posters distributed to theaters and other poster venues (such as bus stops) by the movie studios are never sold directly to the public.
Collecting
Accordingly, most modern posters are not as valuable.
Collecting
However, some recent posters, such as the Pulp Fiction " Lucky Strike " U.S. one-sheet poster (recalled due to a dispute with the cigarette company), are quite rare.
Lobby cards
Lobby cards are similar to posters but smaller, usually 11 in × 14 in (28 cm × 36 cm), also 8 in × 10 in (20 cm × 25 cm) before 1930.
Lobby cards

Although typically issued in sets of eight, with each featuring a different scene from the film, some releases were, in unusual circumstances, promoted with larger (12 cards) or smaller sets (6 cards).
Lobby cards
The set for The Running Man (1963), for example, had only six cards, whereas the set for The Italian Job (1969) had twelve.
Lobby cards
Films released by major production companies experiencing financial difficulties often lacked lobby sets, such as Manhunter (1986).
Lobby cards
A Jumbo Lobby Card is larger, 14 in × 17 in (36 cm × 43 cm) and also issued in sets.
Lobby cards
Prior to 1940 studios promoted major releases with the larger card sets.
Lobby cards
These, however, also refer to black-and-white press photographs, in addition to the more typical 8-by-10-inch promotional devices resembling lobby cards.
Lobby cards
The Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library at Yale University holds a collection of lobby cards from silent western films that date between 1910 and 1930.
Teaser poster
Bearing only a symbol associated with the film, or simply just the title.
Billing block
A billing block can be seen at the bottom of Reynold Brown's poster from Attack of the 50 Foot Woman (1958), which is reproduced below.
Billing block
By convention, the point size of the billing block is 25 or 35 percent of the average height of each letter in the title logo.
Awards

The Hollywood Reporter defines the term "key art" as "the singular, iconographic image that is the foundation upon which a movie's marketing campaign is built." In 2006, the original poster for The Silence of the Lambs was named best film poster "of the past 35 years".

memo_hopalong_cassidee_lunchbox.title: Hopalong Cassidy
sents: lead
Hopalong Cassidy is a fictional cowboy hero created in 1904 by the author Clarence E.
lead
Mulford, who wrote a series of short stories and novels based on the character.
lead
Mulford portrayed the character as rude, dangerous, and rough-talking.
lead
He was shot in the leg during a gun fight which caused him to walk with a little "hop", hence the nickname.
lead

From the 1930s to the 1950s, the character became indelibly associated with actor William Boyd, who portrayed Cassidy first in a series of sixty-six films from 1935 to 1948, then in children-oriented radio and TV series, both of which lasted until 1952.
lead
Boyd's portrayal of Cassidy had little in common with the literary character, being instead a clean-cut, sarsaparilla -drinking hero who never shot first.
lead
The plots of the film, radio and TV series were generally not taken from Mulford's writings.
lead

At the peak of the character's popularity in the early 1950s, he spawned enormous amounts of merchandise, as well as a comic strip, additional novels by Louis L'Amour (writing as Tex Burns), and even a short-lived amusement park, "Hoppyland", in Venice, Los Angeles.
In literature
Mulford wrote the first Hopalong Cassidy short story in 1904 while living in Fryeburg, Maine.
In literature
He wrote the first novel, Bar-20 (named after Cassidy's ranch) in 1906.
In literature
He wrote 28 Hopalong Cassidy novels in all, with the last one, Hopalong Cassidy Serves a Writ, being published in 1941.
In literature
Not all of these novels focused on the Cassidy character; some focused on other characters in and around Bar-20.
In literature
Although they were his first published novels, he was unhappy with the assignment, since he preferred the original character, and publicly denied authorship of the novels for the rest of his life.
In literature
In 2005, author Susie Coffman published Follow Your Stars, new stories starring the character.
Film history

As portrayed on the screen, white-haired Bill "Hopalong" Cassidy was usually clad strikingly in black (including his hat, an exception to the Western film stereotype that only villains wore black hats).
Film history
George Hayes (later to become known as "Gabby" Hayes) originally played Cassidy's grizzled sidekick, Windy Halliday.
Film history
Clyde, the most durable of the sidekicks, remained with the series until it ended.
Film history
The 66 Hopalong Cassidy pictures were filmed by independent producers who released the films through the studios.
Film history
The first "Hoppies", as the films were known, were distributed by Paramount Pictures to favorable returns, and United Artists was the distributor after Paramount.
Film history
Harry Sherman wanted to make more ambitious films and tried to cancel the Cassidy series, but popular demand forced Sherman back into production, this time for United Artists.
Film history
Sherman gave up the series in 1944, but Boyd wanted to keep it going, and ended up co-producing 12 more films himself, from 1946 to 1948, now with lower budgets.
Film history

Captain Midnight (later rebranded on television as Jet Jackson, Flying Commando) is an American adventure franchise first broadcast as a radio serial from 1938 to 1949.
lead

The character's popularity throughout the 1940s and into the mid-1950s extended to serial films (1942), a television show (1954–1956), a syndicated newspaper strip (1942 – late 1940s), and a comic book title (1942–1948).
Radio origins

Developed at the Blackett, Sample and Hummert advertising agency in Chicago, Captain Midnight began as a syndicated show on October 17, 1938, airing through the spring of 1940 on a few Midwest stations, including Chicago's WGN.
Radio origins
In 1940, Ovaltine, a product of The Wander Company, took over sponsorship.
Radio origins
With Pierre Andre as announcer, the series was then heard nationally on the Mutual Radio Network where it remained until 1942.
Radio origins
Government broke up the NBC Red and Blue Networks, Ovaltine moved the series back to Mutual, beginning September 1945, where it remained until December 1949.
Premise
The title character, originally Captain Jim "Red" Albright, was a World War I U.S.
Premise
When the show began in 1938, Albright was a private aviator who helped people, but his situation changed in 1940.
Premise

When the show was taken over by Ovaltine, the origin story explained how Albright was recruited to head the Secret Squadron, an aviation-oriented paramilitary organization fighting sabotage and espionage during the period prior to the United States' entry into World War II.
Premise
The Secret Squadron acted both within and outside the United States.
Premise

When the United States was attacked at Pearl Harbor, which curiously was foreshadowed in the program, the show shifted the Secret Squadron's duties to fight the more unconventional aspects of the war.
Premise
The Secret Squadron wartime activities were usually outside the continental United States, with adventures in Europe, South America, the Pacific, and continental Asia.
Premise
Secret Squadron activities shifted to contending with criminals as well as spies.
Characters
Captain Midnight – World War I aviator who leads the Secret Squadron, though he spends much time in the field actively contending with crime, espionage, and sabotage.
Characters

The Captain is usually accompanied by a team consisting of three Secret Squadron members (played by Ed Prentiss, Bill Bouchey and Paul Barnes, with Ed Prentiss also playing his part as Captain Midnight the longest).
Characters
Chuck Ramsay – Captain Midnight's ward, a young man in his late teens or early twenties who is a Secret Squadron agent.
Characters
Prior to the formation of the Secret Squadron, he shared adventures with his guardian.
Characters
Ichabod "Ikky" Mudd – The Secret Squadron's Chief Mechanic.
Characters
Mudd knew Captain Midnight briefly before the Secret Squadron's formation, and joined the Squadron shortly after it was formed.
Characters
Joyce Ryan – A young woman in her late teens or early twenties who is a Secret Squadron agent.
Characters
She was originally discovered as an amnesiac by Captain Midnight and Chuck Ramsay during a 1941 skirmish with the forces of Ivan Shark.
Characters
Prior to World War II, she regained her memory and elected to remain in the Secret Squadron.
Characters
Agent Kelly, SS-11 – Lyle William Kelly, a Secret Squadron agent who frequently accompanied Captain Midnight's usual team on their adventures.
Characters
Army Intelligence officer recalled from inactive duty as Captain Midnight's superior officer.
Characters
Steele usually worked in the background but often provided the Secret Squadron with data and equipment.
Characters
Jones" – Pseudonym used by the mysterious highly placed government official who created the Secret Squadron and made Captain Midnight its commander, implicitly the President of the United States.
Characters
Baron von Karp – Nazi World War II villain with whom the Secret Squadron contended, first in the United States, then in occupied Europe.
Characters
Admiral Himakito – Japanese officer with whom the Secret Squadron contended in the Pacific theater during World War II.
Film
Popular actor-stunt man Dave O'Brien had the title role in the Columbia Pictures 15-episode serial Captain Midnight (1942).
Film
Missing were the Secret Squadron and the Squadron equipment.
Film
The Captain Midnight character was presented as a masked secret identity for Captain Albright.
Film
The serial was later aired (one chapter per week) on select TV stations in the fall of 1953 and early 1954, under the title Captain Midnight's Adventure Theatre.
Film
(The TV show began a bit later, on September 4, 1954, on a weekly basis on CBS.
Television
The Captain Midnight TV series, produced by Screen Gems and starring Richard Webb, began September 9, 1954, on CBS, continuing for 39 episodes until January 21, 1956.
Television
(The first season ran 26 episodes from September 9, 1954, through February 26, 1955; the second season ran 13 episodes from October 29, 1955, through January 21, 1956).
Television
In the television program, Captain Midnight (now a veteran of the Korean War) heads the Secret Squadron as a private organization, in contrast to the radio show.
Television
As with the Fawcett comic, the only other character of the radio show held over was Ichabod (Ikky) Mudd (played by Sid Melton), who was used for comic relief.
Television
(Soule was the only actor to perform in both the radio program and the television program.
Television
The aircraft featured in the series is the Douglas D-558-2 Skyrocket, named the Silver Dart, and was based on using both models and occasionally stock footage.
Television
Unlike other TV action heroes, Captain Midnight never ventured into space, but rather was confined to Earth's atmosphere.
Television
When the TV series went into syndication in 1958 via Telescreen Advertising, Ovaltine was no longer the sponsor.
Comic strip
A newspaper comic strip, based closely on the radio program, debuted in 1942.
Comic strip
The strip was released by the Chicago Sun Syndicate on June 29, 1942, and ran until the late 1940s.
Comic strip
France Herron wrote the strip from 1942 to 1944.
Comic strip

In the strip, Captain Midnight was referred to as "an unofficial fighter for freedom," which is at variance from the radio show, where the Secret Squadron was set up by a high governmental official ("Mr.
Comic book
Dell Comics published Captain Midnight adventures in The Funnies #57 (Captain Midnight's first appearance in comics), #59, 61–63 (Sept.
Comic book
1942) and Popular Comics #76–78 (June–August 1942).
Comic book
Fawcett published 67 issues of Captain Midnight Comics from Sept.
Comic book
The Fawcett character bore little resemblance to the radio character, and only the character Ichabod Mudd appeared regularly in the comic as the sidekick Sgt.
Comic book
In his Captain Albright secret identity he was a genius-level inventor like Edison.
Comic book
Miller & Son in 40 issues in 1950–1953.
Comic book
In 2010, Moonstone Books ' revival of the Hillman Periodicals 1940s title Air Fighters Comics published its issue #1, which included a new Captain Midnight story.
Comic book
In 2012, Dark Horse Comics reintroduced the character, with a three-part story written by Joshua Williamson with art by Victor Ibañez and Pere Pérez.
Comic book
In June 2013, Captain Midnight #1 was released by the same publisher as an ongoing series.
Books
In 1942 Whitman Publishing released Joyce of the Secret Squadron as part of the Authorized Editions series.
Books
In 2000, McFarland released Radio's Captain Midnight: The Wartime Biography.
Books
In 2010, Moonstone Books published a collection of new Captain Midnight short stories entitled Captain Midnight Chronicles.
Cultural references to Captain Midnight

In the television series The Dick Van Dyke Show, S05 E27 "The Man From My Uncle", Laura says to Rob "Not every adult still holds on to their Captain Midnight decoder ring" when speaking about his boy-like excitement for the FBI using their home as a stakeout base of operations.
Cultural references to Captain Midnight
The 1977 short story "Jeffty Is Five" by Harlan Ellison prominently features the main characters bonding over Captain Midnight broadcasts and owning Secret Decoder Badges.
Cultural references to Captain Midnight

In Stephen King 's 1986 horror novel It, during the Losers Club's first underground battle with It in 1958, Maturin the turtle references protagonist Bill Denbrough believing in the existence of Captain Midnight while aiding him in the first Ritual of Chud.
Cultural references to Captain Midnight

In the television series Miami Vice S03 E13 "Down for the Count, Part 2", Tubbs tells Crockett "And I don't even have my Captain Midnight decoder ring" when they discuss a letter with encrypted information.
Cultural references to Captain Midnight
A hacker using the pseudonym of "Captain Midnight" hacked the HBO signal in 1986.
Cultural references to Captain Midnight
In the 2018 film The House with a Clock in its Walls, both the young hero and the villain are fans of Captain Midnight.
Cultural references to Captain Midnight
In Season 5, Episode 10 of The Beverly Hillbillies, Max Baer, Jr. as Jethro is piloting the O.K Oil Company corporate jet while wearing an aviator’s helmet with goggles and a leather jacket.

memo_the_jetsams_lunchbox.title: The Jetsons
sents: lead
The Jetsons is an American animated sitcom produced by Hanna-Barbera Productions.
lead
It originally aired in prime time from September 23, 1962, to March 17, 1963, on ABC, then later aired in reruns via syndication, with new episodes produced from 1985 to 1987.
lead
It was Hanna-Barbera's Space Age counterpart to The Flintstones.
lead

While the Flintstones lived in a world which was a comical version of the Stone Age, with machines powered by birds and dinosaurs, the Jetsons live in a comical version of a century in the future, with elaborate robotic contraptions, aliens, holograms, and whimsical inventions.
lead
The original had 24 episodes and aired on Sunday nights on ABC beginning on September 23, 1962, with prime time reruns continuing through September 22, 1963.
lead
It debuted as the first program broadcast in color on ABC, back in the early 1960s when only a handful of ABC stations were capable of broadcasting in color.
lead
In contrast, The Flintstones, while always produced in color, was broadcast in black-and-white for its first two seasons.
lead
The show was originally scheduled opposite Walt Disney's Wonderful World of Color and Dennis the Menace and did not receive much attention.
Voice cast

(in "The Space Car"), Bank Teller (in "The Space Car"), Molecular Motors Video Announcer (in "The Space Car"), Bank Security Guard #2 (in "The Space Car"), Moonstone (in "The Space Suit", "Astro's Top Secret"), Professor Lunar (in "Test Pilot"), Mr.
Voice cast
Bergman completed voice work as George and Spacely for Jetsons: The Movie (1990) after George O'Hanlon and Mel Blanc died during production.
Additional voices
Michael Bell (Season 2) as Robot Desk Sergeant (in "Crime Games"), Rocky Retro (in "9 to 5 to 9"), Mr.
Additional voices
Brian Cummings (Seasons 2-3) as Robot Doctor (in "Father/Daughter Dance"), Robot DJ (in "Father/Daughter Dance"), Mr.
Additional voices

Allan Melvin (Season 2) as Solarini (in "Fugitive Fleas"), Mangler Mars (in "Astro's Big Moment"), Marsley (in "The Jetson Christmas Carol"), Ghost of Christmas Present (in "The Jetson Christmas Carol"), Mr.
Additional voices
Tweeter (in "Jane's Driving Lesson", "Rosey Come Home", "9 to 5 to 9"), Fred Solarvan (in "Miss Solar System"), Announcer (in "TV or Not TV"), Boppo Crushcar (in "High Moon"), C.B.
Additional voices
John Stephenson (Seasons 2-3) as Jeffrey (in "Elroy Meets Orbitty"), Police Officer (in "Dance Time"), Director (in "Dance Time"), Dr.
Production
The first season for the series was produced and directed by William Hanna and Joseph Barbera.
Production
Cartoons closed in May 1961, several of its animators, including Gerry Chiniquy and Ken Harris, joined Hanna-Barbera to work on the first season.
Morey Amsterdam and Pat Carroll controversy

In 1963, Morey Amsterdam and Pat Carroll each filed $12,000 suits against Hanna-Barbera for breach of contract, claiming they had been cast and signed to the roles of George Jetson and Jane Jetson, respectively.
Morey Amsterdam and Pat Carroll controversy
Although their contracts stipulated they would be paid US$500 an episode with a guarantee of twenty-four episodes (i.e., a full season) of work, they recorded only one episode before being replaced.
Morey Amsterdam and Pat Carroll controversy
In a 2013 interview, Pat Carroll indicated that the court had ruled in favor of Hanna-Barbera.
Episodes
The show's original run consisted of 24 episodes that first aired on ABC from September 23, 1962, to March 17, 1963, and, as was standard practice at the time, contained a laugh track.
Episodes

In 1984, Hanna-Barbera began producing new episodes specifically for syndication; by September 1985, the 24 episodes from the first season were combined with 41 new episodes and began airing in morning or late afternoon time slots in 80 U.S. media markets, including the 30 largest.
Episodes
The 41 new episodes were produced at a cost of $300,000 each, and featured all of the voice actors from the 1962–1963 show.
Episodes
During 1987, 10 additional "season 3" episodes were also made available for syndication.
Broadcast history
Following its prime time cancellation, ABC placed reruns of The Jetsons on its Saturday morning schedule for the 1963–1964 season.
Broadcast history
The program would spend the next two decades on Saturday mornings, with subsequent runs on CBS (1964–65 and 1969–71) and NBC (1965–67; 1971–76; 1979–81 and 1982–83).
Broadcast history
The Jetsons began airing in syndication in September 1976, and these runs continued after the program returned to NBC's Saturday morning schedule.
Broadcast history
On February 21, 2021, The Jetsons began airing on MeTV.
Theme song
The series' theme song, by composer Hoyt Curtin, became a pop hit in 1986.
Science fiction themes
Lehman considers that the series shares its main science fiction theme with Funderful Suburbia (1962), a Modern Madcaps animated short.
Science fiction themes
Life in outer space is depicted as a fact of life, and the reasons behind humanity's takeover of outer space are never explained.
Science fiction themes
Smithsonian's Matt Novak, in an article called "Why The Show Still Matters" asserts, "Today The Jetsons stands as the single most important piece of 20th century futurism."
Reception

After the announcement of the fall 1962 network television schedule Time magazine characterized The Jetsons as one of several new situation comedies (along with The Beverly Hillbillies, I'm Dickens...
Reception

In 2017, Devon Maloney from The Verge described the show as a "bone-chilling dystopia", stating how a reboot-comic book revealed that an environmental apocalypse caused humans to seek refuge in aerial cities.
Differences between versions
In the first episode of the 1980s episodes, an alien named Orbitty joined the family after Elroy discovered him on a field trip to an asteroid.
Differences between versions
Various appliances appear in the 1980s episodes such as Memo-Minder and Di-Di, Judy's diary, which is shaped like a giant pair of wax lips.
Differences between versions
The original 1960s episodes are distinguished by 1960s design motifs, music, and references (similar to The Flintstones and other Hanna-Barbera shows of that period).
Differences between versions
The 1980s version had a custom soundtrack with new sound-effects created by synthesizer.
Differences between versions
Whereas the 1960s stories were basically 1950s sitcom plots in a setting, the 1980s stories delved into fantastic, sci-fi cartoon territory.
Differences between versions
The 1960s version was more adult-oriented than the 1980s version, which was aimed at younger viewers.
Differences between versions
The 1980s opening credits contain a re-recorded version of the original Jetsons theme song, which features the use of synthesized drums and synth lead tracks typical of 1980s music.
Differences between versions
The 1960s closing credits were similar to the closing credits scenes from The Flintstones, which feature the family getting ready for bed as well as a disaster with their pets.
Differences between versions

The 1960s episodes were rereleased with the redesigned closing segment (containing fewer production staff credits than the 1980s episodes, but has more names than the original closing scene which left several people uncredited) but are usually seen rebroadcast with their original credits segment.
Differences between versions
When the 1980s episodes were made, title cards were also made for the 1960s episodes, which explains the appearance of Orbitty in the title cards of the 1960s episodes.
Differences between versions
Many of the 1980s episodes were colored and composited using computer animation technology including digital ink and paint, rather than the more traditional ink and paint on cels.
Differences between versions
The backgrounds in the 1980s version contain vivid colors, and are more detailed than the 1960s version.
Differences between versions

While the 1960s episodes referenced rockets and other " space age " theme devices, reflective of the real-life American space program which fascinated the United States, the 1980s episodes leaned more towards how computers would influence life in outer space.
Differences between versions
In the 1980s version, Rosie the Robot appears more often than in the 1960s (when she only appeared in two episodes).
Differences between versions
The original spelling of Rosie's name is "Rosey", as featured in the 1962 premiere "Rosey the Robot".
Differences between versions
Instead of the buttons, knobs, dials, and switches in the 1960s version, the 1980s version uses flat buttons and brightly lit consoles.
Differences between versions
The 1960s episodes were fitted with a laugh track (as was The Flintstones); the 1980s episodes were not.
Differences between versions
Many of the 1980s episodes were released in stereo sound, a first for series starring classic Hanna-Barbera characters.
Proposed continuations and reboots
A 1974 proposal would have created a sequel series to The Jetsons, set roughly ten years after the original series.
Proposed continuations and reboots
CBS rejected the proposal and it was retooled into Partridge Family 2200 A.D.
Proposed continuations and reboots
Paramount Pictures first tried to film a live-action version of The Jetsons in 1985, which was to be executive produced by Gary Nardino, but failed to do so.
Proposed continuations and reboots
In the late 1980s, Universal Pictures purchased the film rights for The Flintstones and The Jetsons from Hanna-Barbera Productions.
Proposed continuations and reboots
The result was Jetsons: The Movie, which was released in 1990.
Proposed continuations and reboots
In November 2001, screenwriting duo Paul Foley and Dan Forman were brought onboard to revise a screenplay, with Rob Minkoff attached as director and Denise Di Novi as producer.
Proposed continuations and reboots
On March 18, 2003, it was announced that the script was again being reworked, with Adam Shankman entering negotiations to direct and co-write the film.
Proposed continuations and reboots
In June 2004, with Shankman still onboard as director, Di Novi confirmed that the latest draft was penned by Sam Harper.
Proposed continuations and reboots

In May 2007, director Robert Rodriguez entered talks with Universal Studios and Warner Bros. to film a CGI adaptation of The Jetsons for a potential 2009 theatrical release, having at the time discussed directing a film adaptation of Land of the Lost with Universal.
Proposed continuations and reboots
In February 2012, Warner Bros. hired Van Robichaux and Evan Susser to rewrite the script.
Proposed continuations and reboots
On January 23, 2015, it was announced that Warner Bros. is planning a new animated Jetsons feature film, with Matt Lieberman to provide the screenplay.
Proposed continuations and reboots
As of May 25, 2017, Conrad Vernon will direct the film.
Proposed continuations and reboots
On August 17, 2017, ABC ordered a pilot for a live-action sitcom version of The Jetsons to be written by Gary Janetti and executive produced by Janetti, Jack Rapke and Robert Zemeckis.
Other projects
In the late 1990s, George, Jane, and Astro appeared in Christmas -season commercials for Radio Shack.
Other projects
In 2003, New Zealand ISP Xtra used The Jetsons as part of an advertising campaign, with George Jetson promoting the benefits of broadband Internet.
Other projects
The advert ended with George saying, "Broadband is the way, but some people will never get used to progress", and an image of Fred Flintstone using a stone shaped computer with a real mouse.
Other projects

The Jetsons have appeared in Family Guy three times, on " Brian in Love " (s2, ep4, May 7, 2000), " From Method to Madness " (s4, ep18, January 24, 2002), and on " Meet the Quagmires " (s5, ep18, May 20, 2007).
Other projects
The Jetsons can be seen in the background in the " MetLife " commercial "Everyone" in 2012.
Other projects
The Jetsons appear in Harvey Birdman, Attorney at Law, in the episode "Back to the Present" (s2, ep6, May 16, 2004).
Other projects
The Jetsons family makes a cameo appearance in the 2021 film Space Jam: A New Legacy.
Home media
In 1990, Hanna-Barbera Home Video released six episodes from the show on videocassette.
Home media
Warner Home Video released season 1 on DVD in Region 1 on May 11, 2004; upon its release, James Poniewozik wrote that it is "as much about New Frontier 1962 as about the distant future.
Home media
Season Two, Volume 1 was released on DVD almost three years later, on June 2, 2009, for Region 1.
Home media
On November 8, 2011, Warner Home Video (via the Warner Archive Collection) released The Jetsons: Season 2, Volume 2 on DVD in Region 1 as part of their Hanna-Barbera Classic Collection.
Home media
Warner Archive followed up by releasing Season 3 in the same way on May 13, 2014.
Home media

The complete ABC series was released on Blu-ray on September 10, 2019, by Warner Home Video (again via the Warner Archive Collection), sourced from new 2K scans of the original broadcast masters while maintaining the show's original 4:3 aspect ratio.
Legacy

While satirizing Space Age notions of a better tomorrow, the series seems also to have visually codified expectations of the future to a great many viewers: when the twenty-first century arrived, complaints that flying cars and jet packs were missing often mentioned The Jetsons.".
Legacy
Boomerang has aired reruns of the show since April 1, 2000.
Legacy
Cartoon Network aired the show from 1992 to 2004 and returned the series October 2012.
Legacy
Also, some of the 1980s episodes were available for viewing on In2TV prior to its shutdown; these episodes were later moved to the online version of Kids' WB.
Legacy
The Kids' WB website eventually shut down in 2015, however, the Kids' WB episodes can still be streamed, thanks to much of the website being preserved by the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine.
Legacy
Forbes magazine valued Spacely Sprockets at $1.3 billion, on its "The 25 Largest Fictional Companies" list.
Legacy

The original cartoon series had several devices that did not exist at the time but subsequently have not only been invented but are in common usage: a flatscreen television, newspaper on a computer -like screen, a computer virus, video chat, a tanning bed, home treadmill and more.
Legacy
In January 2009, IGN listed The Jetsons as the 46th best animated television series.

memo_star_wares_lunchbox.title: Star Wars
sents: lead
Star Wars is an American epic space opera media franchise created by George Lucas, which began with the eponymous 1977 film and quickly became a worldwide pop culture phenomenon.
lead

The franchise has been expanded into various films and other media, including television series, video games, novels, comic books, theme park attractions, and themed areas, comprising an all-encompassing fictional universe.
lead
Star Wars is one of the highest-grossing media franchises of all time.
lead

The original 1977 film, retroactively subtitled Episode IV: A New Hope, was followed by the sequels Episode V: The Empire Strikes Back (1980) and Episode VI: Return of the Jedi (1983), forming the original Star Wars trilogy.
lead

Lucas later returned to the series to write and direct a prequel trilogy, consisting of Episode I: The Phantom Menace (1999), Episode II: Attack of the Clones (2002), and Episode III: Revenge of the Sith (2005).
lead
In 2012, Lucas sold his production company to Disney, relinquishing his ownership of the franchise.
lead
This led to a sequel trilogy, consisting of Episode VII: The Force Awakens (2015), Episode VIII: The Last Jedi (2017), and Episode IX: The Rise of Skywalker (2019).
lead
All nine films, collectively referred to as the " Skywalker Saga ", were nominated for Academy Awards, with wins going to the first two releases.
Premise
Virtually any Earth biome, along with many fictional ones, has its counterpart as a Star Wars planet which, in most cases, teem with sentient and non-sentient alien life.
Premise
While Jedi Knights can be numerous, the Dark Lords of the Sith (or 'Darths') are intended to be limited to two: a master and their apprentice.
The Skywalker Saga
The saga was produced non-chronologically, beginning in media res with the release of the original trilogy between 1977 and 1983.
Original trilogy
After directing American Graffiti (1973), he wrote a two-page synopsis, which 20th Century Fox decided to invest in.
Original trilogy
By 1974, he had expanded the story into the first draft of a screenplay.
Original trilogy
Fox expected the film would be of limited financial success, and so it was given a relatively low budget, with production being moved to Elstree Studios in England to help save on cost.
Original trilogy
Star Wars was released on May 25, 1977, and first subtitled Episode IV: A New Hope in the 1979 book The Art of Star Wars.
Original trilogy
Episode V: The Empire Strikes Back was released on May 21, 1980, also achieving wide financial and critical success.
Original trilogy
The final film in the trilogy, Episode VI: Return of the Jedi, was released on May 25, 1983.
Prequel trilogy
In 1980, Lucas confirmed that he had the nine-film series plotted, but due to the stress of producing the original trilogy, he had decided to cancel further sequels by 1981.
Prequel trilogy
In 1983, Lucas explained that "There was never a script completed that had the entire story as it exists now...
Prequel trilogy
Technical advances in the late 1980s and early 1990s, including the ability to create computer-generated imagery (CGI), inspired Lucas to consider that it might be possible to revisit his saga.
Prequel trilogy
A theatrical rerelease of the original trilogy in 1997 " updated " the 20-year-old films with the style of CGI envisioned for the new trilogy.
Prequel trilogy
Episode I: The Phantom Menace was released on May 19, 1999, Episode II: Attack of the Clones on May 16, 2002, and Episode III: Revenge of the Sith on May 19, 2005.
Prequel trilogy
The first two films were met with mixed reviews, with the third being received somewhat more positively.
Sequel trilogy
Lucas provided Kennedy his story treatments for the sequels during the 2012 sale, but in 2015 it was revealed Lucas's sequel outline had been discarded.
Sequel trilogy
Episode VII: The Force Awakens was released on December 16, 2015, Episode VIII: The Last Jedi on December 13, 2017, and Episode IX: The Rise of Skywalker on December 18, 2019, in many countries.
Standalone films

The first film released was 2016's Rogue One, which tells the story of the rebels who steal the plans for the Death Star, the Galactic Empire 's superweapon, just before the events of the original Star Wars film.
Standalone films
A second film, 2018's Solo, tells Han Solo's backstory, set 10 years prior to A New Hope.
Standalone films
The series Obi-Wan Kenobi was originally planned as a film, but changed to a limited series due to Solo underperforming at the box office.
Upcoming films
The Mandalorian & Grogu is scheduled for release on May 22, 2026.
Other potential projects
Untitled Rian Johnson trilogy: In November 2017, a trilogy of movies written by The Last Jedi writer/director Rian Johnson was announced to be in development.
Other potential projects
By May 2019, the duo were also slated to serve as co-directors of the first installment in their three films.
Other potential projects
In January 2024, the filmmaking duo announced that the working title was The First Jedi and would have followed the titular ancient protagonist.
Other potential projects
Untitled Shawn Levy film: In November 2022, Shawn Levy entered talks to direct a Star Wars film, following his work on Deadpool & Wolverine (2024) and the fifth and final season of Stranger Things.
Other potential projects
In September 2023, Levy said that development on his Star Wars film began, but would not continue until after the conclusion of the 2023 Writers Guild of America strike.
Animated series
The first two animated series, Droids and Ewoks, were produced in the 1980s.
Animated series
Following Disney's acquisition of Lucasfilm, all animated series released prior to 2014, apart from the 2008 series, were discarded from the franchise's canon.
Animated series
Subsequent animated series include Rebels, released in 2014; Resistance, released in 2018; and The Bad Batch, released in 2021.
Live-action series
The first series, The Mandalorian, was released in 2019 for the streaming service Disney+ and is set between the original and sequel trilogies of the Skywalker Saga.
Live-action series

Due to its success, the series spawned multiple live-action spin-offs set during the same fictional era, including The Book of Boba Fett, released in 2021; Ahsoka, released in 2023; and the upcoming Skeleton Crew.
Fictional timeline
Rise of the First Order: The remnants of the Empire transform into the First Order but are fought by the Resistance, climaxing with the defeat of Palpatine and the Sith by the Jedi Rey.
Fictional timeline

lead

Known for their face paint and stage outfits, the group rose to prominence in the mid-1970s with shock rock -style live performances which featured fire-breathing, blood-spitting, smoking guitars, shooting rockets, levitating drum kits and pyrotechnics.
lead
The band went through several lineup changes, with Stanley and Simmons remaining the only consistent members.
lead
The final lineup consisted of them, Tommy Thayer (lead guitar, vocals) and Eric Singer (drums, vocals).
lead

With their makeup and costumes, the band members took on the personas of comic book-style characters: the Starchild (Stanley), the Demon (Simmons), the Spaceman or Space Ace (Frehley), and the Catman (Criss).
lead
During the second half of the 1970s, Kiss became one of America's most successful rock bands and a pop culture phenomenon.
lead
Due to creative differences, Criss departed the band in 1980, followed by Frehley in 1982.
lead

memo_happy_meel_circus_wagon.title: Happy Meal
sents: lead
A Happy Meal is a kids' meal usually sold at the American fast food restaurant chain McDonald's since June 1979.
lead
A small toy or book is included with the food, both of which are usually contained in a red cardboard box with a yellow smiley face and the McDonald's logo.
lead
The packaging and toy are frequently part of a marketing tie-in to an existing television series, film or toyline.
History
In the mid-1970s, Yolanda Fernández de Cofiño began working with her husband operating McDonald's restaurants in Guatemala.
History
In 1977, the McDonald's restaurant owner clients who regularly met with Bernstein were looking for ways to create a better dining experience for families with kids.
History
Bernstein then named it the Happy Meal and it was successfully introduced with television and radio spots and in-store posters in the Kansas City market in October 1977.
History
Other markets followed and the national roll-out happened in 1979.
History
Bernstein received Trademark #1136758 (Serial #73148046) for his idea in 1977 which he assigned to his client, McDonald's Corporation, on June 10, 1980.
History
McDonald's Happy Meal 10th Anniversary 1977-1987 To Robert A.
History
Your insight and conviction truly has made McDonald's a fun place for children for the past 10 years!
History
The first such promotion was the " Star Trek Meal", which promoted Star Trek: The Motion Picture in December 1979.
History
In 1982, McDonald's recalled Playmobil Happy Meal toys because they could have been dangerous to children under three years of age.
History
In 1992, McDonald's withdrew their range of Happy Meal toys for the film Batman Returns, after complaints from parents that the film was unsuitable for children.
History
In July 2011, McDonald's announced plans to make Happy Meals healthier, including the addition of apples.
History
The redesigned meals would contain a smaller portion (1.1 ounces) of fries, along with the apples.
History

On February 4, 2013, McDonald's announced that Fish McBites (fried Alaskan pollock, the same fish used in Filet-O-Fish) would be added as an entree, which would run until March, intended to coincide with Lent.
History
In 2014, McDonald's introduced a mascot to Happy Meals in the United States named Happy, who originated in France and some international countries as early as 2009.
Happy Meal toy
When the Happy Meal was launched in 1979, the toys were a McDoodle stencil, a McWrist wallet, an ID bracelet, a puzzle lock, a spinning top or a McDonaldland character-shaped eraser.
Happy Meal toy
The Happy Meal toys are designed for ages 2+, while the toddler toys are aimed at 3 and younger.
Bans

On November 2, 2010, the San Francisco Board of Supervisors passed a law requiring that children's meals sold in restaurants must meet certain nutritional standards before they could be sold with toys.
Bans

The law, urged in part by an increase of childhood obesity in the United States, would allow toys to be included with children's meals that have fewer than 600 calories and fewer than 640 milligrams of sodium, contain fruits and vegetables, and include beverages without excessive fat or sugar.
Bans
The board overturned the veto of Mayor Gavin Newsom on November 23, 2010, to pass the law.
Bans
McDonald's circumvented the ban by charging 10 cents for the toys.
Bans
A class action lawsuit seeking to ban Happy Meal toys in California was filed in 2010.
Bans
In Chile, the Happy Meal, along with kids' meals at other fast food chains, no longer includes free toys, in response to a 2012 law banning such toys in a move to prevent obesity.
2004 Active Fit Happy Meal
An adult version of the Happy Meal was released in 2004 with McDonald's "Active Fit" Happy Meal.
2022 Cactus Plant Flea Market collaboration
In 2022 another adult version of the Happy Meal was released as a limited release collaboration with Cactus Plant Flea Market.
2023 Kerwin Frost collaboration
Following the success of the 2022 promotion, McDonald's launched another adult Happy Meal promotion the following year, this time in collaboration with Kerwin Frost.
2023 Kerwin Frost collaboration
The 2023 edition features the same choices of meals along with figurines of the McNugget Buddies, with updated designs from Frost.

memo_garbage_pale_kids_wax_pack.title: Garbage Pail Kids

Inventor(s): Art Spiegelman, Mark Newgarden and John Pound

sents: lead
Garbage Pail Kids is a series of sticker trading cards produced by the Topps Company, originally released in 1985 and designed to parody the Cabbage Patch Kids dolls, which were popular at the time.
lead

Each sticker card features a Garbage Pail Kid character having some comical abnormality, deformity, and/or suffering a terribly painful fate/death with a humorous word play character name such as Adam Bomb or Blasted Billy.
lead
Two versions of each card were produced, with variations featuring the same artwork but a different character name, differentiated by an "a" or "b" letter following the card number.
lead
The sticker fronts are die-cut so that just the character with its nameplate and the GPK logo can be peeled from the backing.
lead

Many of the card backs feature puzzle pieces that form giant murals, while other flip-side subjects vary greatly among the various series, from humorous licenses and awards to comic strips and, in more recent releases, humorous Facebook profiles.
lead
Fifteen original series (OS) of regular trading cards were released in the United States, with various sets released in other countries.
lead
Two large-format card editions were also released, as well as a set of fold-out posters.
lead

All-New Series (ANS) sets were introduced in 2003, Flashback re-releases began in 2010 and a Brand-New Series (BNS) was announced for 2012 with Brand New Series 2, Chrome S1, and BNS3 following in 2013.
History
The concept originally began as an unreleased Wacky Packages sticker for a 1985 series, but the management at Topps thought it would be a good idea for a separate spin-off series.
History

Spiegelman and fellow cartoonist Mark Newgarden worked together as the editors and art directors of the project, Len Brown was the manager and the first run of the cards was drawn exclusively by artist John Pound.
Variations
Initially in New Zealand, a Series 6 of the Garbage Pail Kids was released as a market test (this version was a mix of the United States Series 6 and 7).
Variations
After this success, Series 1 was released in Australia and New Zealand known as The Garbage Gang and was identical to the United States version (albeit smaller in size).
Variations

The first series was released in Australia and New Zealand in 1989 with different versions: the Australian stickers were darker, had a different banner and some of the names were changed to reflect cultural differences.
Variations
From Series 2 onward, the same version was released in Australia and New Zealand.
Variations
Series 4 was the last release of The Garbage Gang.
Commercial success
The commercial success of the trading cards led to the production of a live-action movie, The Garbage Pail Kids Movie, in 1987.
Commercial success
An animated television series was also created in 1987, but its initial scheduled broadcast in the U.S. was postponed due to parental complaints.
Commercial success
The show did make a brief appearance on U.S. television years after it was originally intended to air and was also briefly aired in Europe.
Commercial success

The movie was released on DVD by MGM Home Entertainment on July 12, 2005 (the original VHS had been distributed by Paramount) and the animated TV series was later also released on DVD by CBS Home Entertainment on April 4, 2006 (again with distribution by Paramount).
Commercial success
A similar set of 160 trading cards, called The Sloppy Slobs, was released in Italy in 1993.
School ban
During the height of the cards' popularity, Garbage Pail Kids were banned in many schools.
Trademark infringement lawsuit
Topps was sued by the rightsholders of Cabbage Patch Kids, Original Appalachian Artworks, for trademark infringement.
Trademark infringement lawsuit
Production of the cards themselves continued, but by 1988 sales had dwindled and a planned Series 16 was never produced.
BTS Bruisers
In March 2021, Topps released a sticker card depicting a Whac-A-Mole game with members of K-pop group BTS being severely beaten with a Grammy award.
All-New Series sets
In 2003, Topps reintroduced Garbage Pail Kids with all-new artwork, dubbed the All-New Series (ANS).
All-New Series sets
ANS1 was entirely made up of artwork intended for release in the 1980s as Series 16, but 2004's ANS2 featured brand-new and original concepts.
All-New Series sets

Unique numbers on the backs of silver foil and gold foil insert cards could be redeemed online at the official Garbage Pail Kids website, where visitors could build and "gross out" their own Garbage Pail Kids; as the number of unique code numbers applied to the character increased, the grosser it became.
All-New Series sets
In 2005, Topps celebrated the 20th anniversary of the GPK franchise with special Sketch Card original art inserts for its ANS4 set.
All-New Series sets

These were limited to one randomly inserted card per hobby-exclusive box (available only from speciality retailers) and featured original artwork by series regulars John Pound, Tom Bunk and Jay Lynch, as well as guest artists Strephon Taylor, John Czop, Don Perlin and Justin Green.
All-New Series sets
Although a regular to the series with over 35 paintings, Luis Diaz was not involved in the sketch cards due to a previous financial dispute with Topps from years earlier.
All-New Series sets
In 2006, ANS5 was released with 40 more new kids (each with an a/b twin), followed by ANS6 in early 2007.
All-New Series sets

January 2008 saw the release of ANS7 which expanded the base set to 55 new characters and was the last set to feature new artwork until 2010's Flashback Series 1 subset of six previously unpublished "lost" kids.
All-New Series sets
The ANS cards differ from the original series (OS) in a number of ways, the most obvious being the upgraded quality of the card stock with a glossy protective surface.
All-New Series sets
The ANS releases also changed the card numbering format: OS cards used a continuous numbering pattern so that each new set would pick up where the last one ended (e.g.
All-New Series sets
OS1 ended at #41a/b and OS2 picked up at #42a/b, while ANS reset the numbering back to #1a/b with each subsequent release).
Flashback re-releases
GPK Flashback Series 3 followed on November 2, 2011, with 65 OS reprints, four more "lost" kids, 10 new WATN? cards, five more 3D cards, 10 more Adam Mania cards, plus artist sketches and parallels.
Book
Topps and Abrams Books released a hardcover book that showcases the first five series.
Book
The cover depicts a pack from the very first series released back in 1985.
Brand-New Series sets
In 2012, Topps announced it would reboot the Garbage Pail Kids franchise with new character and content themes more reminiscent of the original 1980s series in a set called Brand-New Series 1 (BNS1).
Brand-New Series sets
The set was released on October 24, 2012.
Brand-New Series sets

BNS1 features 55 new GPK characters, a reality TV subset, motion cards, mix 'n' match stickers, parallels, artist sketch cards and code cards redeemable for a chance to be painted as a GPK in the next BNS.
Brand-New Series sets
BNS2 was released in March and features 55 new characters, 18 reimagined characters, lenticular cards, glow-in-the-dark cards and folded cards.
Chrome Series sets
In October 2013, Topps re-released the original Series 1 as a metallic chromium card set containing all 41 kids, plus 14 previously unpublished "lost" kids.
Chrome Series sets

On July 30, 2014, Topps re-released 1985's original Series 2 set, plus 13 returning characters from Series 2 characters that have been reimagined in previous Garbage Pail Kids sets also as a set of metallic chromium cards.
2014 Series 1
Topps released a series of all-new cards with brand-new artwork for 2014.
30th Anniversary Series
In July 2015, Topps released the 30th Anniversary Series with 110 a/b cards (220 cards total).
Yearly themed series
After the 30th Anniversary Series, Topps began using a new formula that structured each series with an overall theme divided into subsets focusing on particular topics.
Yearly themed series
In January 2016, As American as Apple Pie In Your Face! put GPKs in situations that parodied American culture.
Yearly themed series
A second 2016 series followed in April called Prime Slime Trashy TV with humorous takes on popular television shows.
Yearly themed series
The first series for 2017 was January's Adam-geddon, which put the Garbage Pail Kids (including some classic kids) in perilous end-times scenarios.
Yearly themed series
Topps announced that the second series for 2017 will arrive in October and be called Battle of the Bands, caricaturing popular music acts and album covers.
35th Anniversary Blockchain Series
In April 2020, Topps announced they will celebrate the 35th anniversary by bringing digital collectible Garbage Pail Kids cards to the Blockchain.
35th Anniversary Blockchain Series
On May 12, 2020, the Garbage Pail Kids card packs launched on the WAX blockchain and were sold out in 28 hours.
35th Anniversary Blockchain Series
Each card is certified authentic, and unique and can never be altered.
35th Anniversary Blockchain Series
This is a limited-edition series and only a finite number of cards were ever created (110,000).
35th Anniversary Blockchain Series
Base: Standard static cards featuring both the "A" and "B" names of all 41 characters from the original Series 1.
35th Anniversary Blockchain Series
Prism: Uncommon cards, these cards feature a prismatic sheen effect; "A" and "B" names of all 41 characters.
35th Anniversary Blockchain Series
Sketch: Rare cards that feature an animated transition from original sketches to final art; "A" and "B" names of all 41 characters.
35th Anniversary Blockchain Series
Collector's Edition: Super rare cards with special animations; four characters available in "A" and "B" names.
35th Anniversary Blockchain Series
The first buyers of Garbage Pail Kids card packs on WAX were automatically entered to win an Ultra-Rare Golden Card.
35th Anniversary Blockchain Series
Only 100 of these Golden Cards will ever be minted.
35th Anniversary Blockchain Series
Golden Cards come in the original 41 characters, each with an "A" name and a "B" name.
The Garbage Pail Kids Movie
On August 21, 1987, a live-action film based on the card characters was released.
The Garbage Pail Kids Movie

Its campy production made it both a critical and commercial flop, opening poorly in 374 theaters with initial receipts of $661,512 and total gross receipts of $1,576,615, making a 60% profit on its $1 million budget.
The Garbage Pail Kids Movie
Topps featured advertisements for the movie on the original Series 9 and 10 box-topper poster and variant wrapper.
Cancelled remake
On March 12, 2012, it was announced that Michael Eisner 's Tornante Company would be producing a new movie based on the Garbage Pail Kids, likely with computer-generated character imagery.
Television
In May 2021, it was announced that a new animated series is in the works at HBO Max, and would be co-produced by Topps, Tornante Company and Danny McBride 's production company Rough House Pictures.
Television
In October 2023, director David Gordon Green confirmed the series is still in development.

memo_pet_rock.title: Pet Rock
sents: lead
Pet Rock is a collectible toy made in 1975 by advertising executive Gary Dahl.
lead
They were rocks packaged in custom cardboard boxes complete with ventilation holes and straw bedding imitating a pet carrier.
lead
The fad lasted about six months, ending after a short increase in sales during the Christmas season of December 1975.
lead
Although by February 1976 they were discounted due to lower sales, Dahl sold over one million Pet Rocks for $4 each, and became a millionaire.
History
Gary Dahl came up with the idea in a bar while listening to his friends complain about their pets; this gave him the idea for the perfect "pet": a rock.
History
Dahl said that they were to be the perfect pets and joked about it with his friends before eventually producing Pet Rocks as toys in 1975.
History
In 2022, the toy company Super Impulse purchased the rights to the Pet Rock, reviving the brand.
History
In the 2020s, Pet Rocks grew in popularity in South Korea as tools for meditation or venting out frustrations.
Legacy
A video of Elmo from Sesame Street shouting at Rocco went viral in early 2022.
Legacy
To promote the film, Sabec Limited released an official Pet Rock video game for Nintendo Switch.
Legacy
A24 produced an official licensed Pet Rock as a tie-in for the film Everything Everywhere All at Once.
Legacy
During the travels of the Perseverance rover on Mars, NASA scientists had observed around Sol 341 (February 4, 2022) that a small rock had dropped into one of its wheels.
Legacy
The rock has since stayed on Perseverance ' s wheel for around 427 sols (439 days) as the rover traveled over 6 miles (9.7 km) on the martian surface.

memo_mystic_8_ball.title: Magic 8 Ball
sents: lead
The Magic 8 Ball is a plastic sphere, made to look like an oversized eight ball, that is used for fortune-telling or seeking advice.
lead
It was invented in 1946 by Albert C.
lead
Carter and Abe Bookman and is manufactured by Mattel.
lead
The user asks a yes–no question to the ball, then turns it over to reveal an answer that floats up into a window.
Origin
The functional component of the Magic 8 Ball was invented by Albert C.
Origin
Carter, who was inspired by a spirit writing device used by his mother Mary, a Cincinnati clairvoyant.
Origin

In 1944, Carter filed for a patent for the cylindrical device, assigning it in 1946 to Bookman, Levinson and another partner in what came to be Alabe Crafts, Inc., combining the founder's names, Albert and Abe.
Origin
Bookman made improvements to The Syco-Slate, and in 1948 it was encased in an iridescent crystal ball.
Origin

Though not successful, the revamped product caught the attention of Chicago's Brunswick Billiards, who in 1950 commissioned Alabe Crafts to make a version in the form of a traditional black-and-white 8 ball, which was possibly inspired by a gag in the 1940 Three Stooges short film, You Nazty Spy!
Cultural impact
Although originally sold as a paperweight, the Magic 8 Ball would remain popular for several decades as both an office toy and a children's toy.
Cultural impact
In 1971, Bookman sold Alabe Crafts, Inc., to Ideal Toys, who marketed the ball firmly at children.
Cultural impact
In 1987, the rights were again sold to Tyco Toys, spurring on another marketing campaign and resurgence in interest.
Cultural impact
Tyco Toys was acquired by Mattel, the current manufacturer, in 1997.
Cultural impact
Despite its numerous owners, the Magic 8 Ball has changed little in design and implementation.
Design and usage
The Magic 8 Ball is a hollow plastic sphere resembling a black-and-white 8 ball.
Design and usage
Inside the ball, a cylindrical reservoir contains a white plastic 20-sided regular icosahedron die floating in approximately 100 ml (3 + 1 ⁄ 2 US fl oz) of alcohol dyed dark blue.
Design and usage
Each of the die's 20 faces has an affirmative, negative, or non-committal statement printed in raised letters.
Design and usage
Although most users shake the ball before turning it upright, the instructions warn against doing so to avoid white bubbles.
Design and usage
While the Magic 8 Ball has undergone very few changes, an addition in 1975 by new owners, Ideal Toy Company, fixed the bubble problem.
Possible answers
A standard Magic 8 Ball has twenty possible answers, including ten affirmative answers (●), five non-committal answers (●), and five negative answers (●).
